name: Zanhar / Zangskar
confidence_why: Tournadre and Suzuki 2023 place Zangskari (Zanhar) in the north-western Tibetic group that has no distinctive suprasegmental features, and Koshal 1976 finds stress non-significant in neighbouring Leh Ladakhi, so no source gives a stress placement for Zangskari and none disagrees that it lacks distinctive stress.

Villejuif: LACITO Publications (CNRS) (open access). Supporting: Koshal, Sanyukta. 1976. Ladakhi Phonetic Reader. Mysore: CIIL, p. 14 (Central/Leh Ladakhi, lada1244).
catalog_locator: Part 2, ch. 9, sec. 9.10.6 'Phonological characteristics of the NW section', subheading 'Suprasegmental features', p. 626; NW-section membership incl. Zanhar: sec. 9.10.2 p. 619; sec. 7.3 p. 235; sec. 7.3.3 'Stress' p. 241.
catalog_quote: Suprasegmental features It is well-known that the Tibetic languages in the NW section do not have distinctive suprasegmental features. However, in Balti for example, the position of stress may affect some phonetic realizations. ... [sec. 9.10.2, p. 619] For the dialect classification of the NW section, we propose the following seven groups: Balti ... Purik ... Nubra ... Sham ... Leh (Central Ladakh) ... Zanhar ... Kharu ... [sec. 7.3, p. 235] However, a few western and eastern Tibetic languages such as Amdo, Ladaks, Purik, Zanhar and Balti do not have any distinctive tones. ... [sec. 7.3.3, p. 241] The distinction of stress is attested mainly in Balti. Caplow (2016) and some other scholars believe that Amdo or even Lhasa also have a stress opposition but it may play a secondary role in the system. The distinction of stress only occurs in polysyllabic words.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Areal statement only: in the North-Western Tibetic dialects (which include Zanhar/Zangskari) stress and tone are not distinctive; stress position is discussed only for Balti (nouns sigma-2 / verbs sigma-1 per sec. 7.3.3), and no position is given for Zangskari. Supporting neighbour-lect statement: Koshal 1976: 14 finds stress and tone 'non-significant' in Leh Ladakhi.
new_statements.exceptions: Balti singled out as a dialect where 'the position of stress may affect some phonetic realizations'; sec. 9.10.2 quotes Zeisler 2011 that the innovative dialects of 'Upper Indus, Changthang, and Zanskar' show cluster reduction 'and tonal features can be found' — a possible tension with the 'no distinctive suprasegmentals' line that only Zeisler 2011 itself could resolve.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about phonemic distinctiveness at dialect-group level, not about word-level stress placement or citation forms; it is not a Zangskari-specific description.
new_statements.identity_note: No Zangskari-specific stress statement was found. The quoted statement (Tournadre & Suzuki 2023: 626) is scoped over the whole 'North-Western section' of Tibetic (Balti, Purik, Nubra, Sham, Leh, Zanhar = Zangskari, Kharu), i.e. it covers zang1248 only as one member of a dialect group. The supporting statement in Koshal 1976: 14 describes Central/Leh Ladakhi (lada1244), in a work that treats 'Zanskar Ladakhi' as a regional variety with 'minor phonological and lexical differences'. Zeisler 2011 classifies Zangskari with the Kenhat (Upper Ladakh) dialects, which she describes as partly innovative with 'tonal features' — so a Leh-Ladakhi or Balti stress statement should not be transferred to zang1248 without a Kenhat/Zanskar-specific source.

sources.note: Sec. 9.10.6 p.626 (NW section = Balti, Purik, Nubra, Sham, Leh, Zanhar, Kharu): 'the Tibetic languages in the NW section do not have distinctive suprasegmental features. However, in Balti for example, the position of stress may affect some phonetic realizations.' Sec. 7.3.3 p.241-242: stress distinction 'attested mainly in Balti'. Nothing specific on stress position in Zanhar/Zangskari; Zanhar-specific remarks are all segmental (fricativisation, loss of final -s, diphthongs).

sources.note: This work describes Ladakhi and Balti (as a pair, contrasted with chosskat / Old Tibetan / Amdo Tibetan); Zangskar is never named. The paper is a 7-page conference abstract (printed pp. 27-33) of Zeisler 2005 (Ladakhi Histories, Brill, 41-64) on the genealogical position of Ladakhi and Balti, plus an appendix summarising Róna-Tas 1985 on the origin of the Tibetan script. The words stress, accent, tone, pitch, prosody do not occur. Zangskar / Zanskar is not mentioned.
